15.0.big: A gene is a stretch of DNA with instructions for making an RNA or protein. This chapter shows how cells read those instructions.
points: Genetic testing raises real questions about privacy and fairness.
In the U.S., the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (2008) bans health insurers and employers from discriminating based on your genes.

15.1.big: Central Dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein. The genetic code reads mRNA three letters (one codon) at a time.
points: 4 bases, read in groups of 3, give 43 = 64 codons for 20 amino acids. Pairs of bases (42 = 16) wouldn't be enough.
The code is degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon, which softens the effect of many mutations.
AUG is the start codon (methionine). UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.
The code is universal: almost every organism uses the same code, which is strong evidence for a common origin.
Exceptions: HIV (a retrovirus) copies RNA back into DNA with reverse transcriptase. Flu viruses copy RNA to RNA.

15.2.big: In bacteria, RNA polymerase binds a promoter, unwinds the DNA, builds mRNA 5'→3', and stops at a terminator.
points: Only the template strand is read. The mRNA matches the nontemplate strand, except with U instead of T.
The σ (sigma) subunit finds the promoter's −35 and −10 (TATAAT) sequences. Without σ, the polymerase would start in random places.
Ending: rho-dependent termination (a protein knocks the polymerase off) or rho-independent termination (the mRNA folds into a GC-rich hairpin).
No nucleus means bacteria can transcribe and translate the same mRNA at the same time.

15.3.big: Eukaryotic transcription works the same basic way, but with three RNA polymerases, complex promoters, and lots of transcription factors.
points: Pol I (nucleolus) makes most rRNAs. Pol II makes all protein-coding pre-mRNAs. Pol III makes tRNAs, 5S rRNA and small RNAs.
Death-cap mushroom poison (α-amanitin) blocks pol II strongly, pol III partly, and pol I not at all.
Promoters include a TATA box (about −30), plus CAAT and GC boxes. TFII transcription factors assemble first and then recruit pol II.
Enhancers and silencers fine-tune how much a gene is transcribed.
The FACT complex moves histones out of the way as the polymerase moves along.

15.4.big: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA gets edited before it leaves the nucleus: a cap, a tail, and splicing.
points: 5' cap (7-methylguanosine): protects the mRNA and helps ribosomes find it.
3' poly-A tail (about 200 A's): more protection, and it helps export the mRNA.
Splicing: spliceosomes cut out introns (in-the-way parts) and join exons (expressed parts) with single-nucleotide precision.
Alternative splicing joins exons in different combinations, so one gene can make several proteins.
tRNAs and rRNAs are trimmed and methylated. tRNAs fold so the anticodon is at one end and the amino acid at the other.
15.4.tip: Exons are expressed. Introns are in the way and get cut out.

15.5.big: Translation: a ribosome reads the mRNA codon by codon while tRNAs bring the matching amino acids, linking them into a polypeptide.
points: Aminoacyl tRNA synthetases (at least 20, one per amino acid) load each tRNA with its correct amino acid.
Initiation: the small subunit finds the start (Shine-Dalgarno sequence in bacteria, the 5' cap and Kozak sequence in eukaryotes). The initiator tRNA (Met) pairs with AUG, and the large subunit joins.
Elongation: tRNAs enter the A site, the growing chain sits in the P site, and empty tRNAs leave from the E site. Peptidyl transferase, which is rRNA, forms each peptide bond.
Termination: a stop codon brings in a release factor, and the protein is let go.
Afterwards, proteins fold (sometimes with chaperones), get modified, and follow signal sequences to where they belong.

1.why: DNA → mRNA → protein. tRNA helps, but it isn't a step in the flow of information.

2.why: The DNA (from virus A) carries the instructions, so the new viruses have A's DNA and A's protein coat.

3.why: More than one codon for the same amino acid means the code is degenerate.

5.why: Proteins are the product of genetic information. They don't store it the way DNA and RNA do.

6.why: mRNA is a temporary working copy. The original (DNA) stays safe in the nucleus.

7.why: The σ (sigma) subunit recognizes the promoter, so transcription starts in the right place.

8.why: "Consensus" means similar across bacterial species, not identical.

9.why: The terminator sequence ends transcription. A stop codon ends translation.

10.why: It depends on the gene: rho-independent genes stop with a hairpin and don't need rho.

11.why: Both have a TATA box (TATAAT in bacteria at −10, TATAAAA in eukaryotes).

12.why: TFII factors build the preinitiation complex during initiation.

13.why: Polymerase III makes 5S rRNA, tRNAs and small RNAs.

14.why: Pol II is extremely sensitive to α-amanitin, and it makes the pre-mRNAs.

15.why: The nucleus separates them: eukaryotes transcribe in the nucleus and translate in the cytoplasm, so the two don't happen at the same time.

16.why: The poly-A tail goes on the 3' end, while the transcript is still in the nucleus.

17.why: Ribosomes recognize the 5' cap to start translation.

18.why: rRNAs are made and assembled in the nucleolus.

19.why: Adding methyl groups (methylation) stabilizes pre-tRNAs and pre-rRNAs.

20.why: Introns are untranslated stretches inside a gene that get spliced out.

21.why: AUG codes for methionine, so that's usually the first amino acid.

22.why: At least one for each of the 20 amino acids.

23.why: Prokaryotes have no ER or nucleus, so their ribosomes are in the cytoplasm.

24.why: Peptidyl transferase is ribosomal RNA, an RNA enzyme.

25.why: Without the cap, the mRNA isn't protected and gets broken down once it reaches the cytoplasm (and ribosomes couldn't recognize it either).

26.why: In eukaryotes, the sequence around the start AUG (Kozak's sequence) helps position the ribosome. Shine-Dalgarno is the bacterial version.

27.why: They match except that RNA uses U wherever DNA has T, so they're never truly identical.

28.why: 43 = 64 isn't enough for 200 amino acids, but 44 = 256 is. So codons would need to be 4 letters long.

29.why: HIV goes RNA → DNA (reverse transcription) → RNA → protein. Flu goes RNA → RNA and never uses DNA.

30.why: Codons: ATG-CGT-TAT-CGG-GAG-TAG becomes ATG-CGT-TAT-GGG-GAG-TAG. The 4th codon changes from CGG (arginine) to GGG (glycine), so it's a missense mutation: one amino acid swapped, and the rest of the protein is the same.

31.why: The core enzyme is α, α, β and β′. Adding σ, which is only needed to start, makes the full holoenzyme.

32.why: Rho-dependent: the polymerase stalls at a run of G's and the rho protein knocks it off. Rho-independent: a GC-rich stretch folds into a hairpin that stalls the polymerase.

33.why: The key structure is the mRNA hairpin, used in rho-independent termination.

34.why: Initiation differs the most: eukaryotes need transcription factors, enhancers and a preinitiation complex, and have to deal with histones.

35.why: Yes: test the polymerase with α-amanitin. Pol I ignores it, pol II is blocked strongly, and pol III partly.

36.why: Alternative splicing lets one gene make several proteins, so you don't need a separate gene for every protein.

37.why: Eukaryotic mRNA has to be processed and exported out of the nucleus before it can be translated.

38.why: No cap means no protection, so the mRNA is broken down once it reaches the cytoplasm.

39.why: mRNA = 5'-AUG GCC GGU UAU UAA GCA-3'. That gives Met-Ala-Gly-Tyr, then UAA = stop: MAGY.

40.why: rRNA in the large subunit catalyzes peptide bonds. RNA acting as an enzyme supports the idea that RNA came before proteins.

41.why: The ribosome matches anticodon to codon. It never checks the amino acid, so the tRNA still pairs with the codon its anticodon matches (and puts the wrong amino acid in).

42.why: Nearly every organism uses the same code, which points to one shared ancestor.

43.why: DNA replication copies the genetic material to pass on.

44.why: Both use RNA polymerase, recognize consensus sequences in promoters, and can end with a hairpin loop.

45.why: The plasma (cytoplasmic) membrane has no DNA. The nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts all do.

46.why: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA, which runs the dogma backwards.

47.why: Labeled thymidine goes into new DNA, found in the nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts. The plasma membrane has no DNA.

48.why: Introns were spliced out of the mRNA, so it's shorter than the gene.

49.why: A weaker promoter means less transcription, so less globin is made.

50.why: 1: UCG GCA AAU UUA GUU = Ser-Ala-Asn-Leu-Val. 2: UCU is also Ser, so it's the same. 3: UAA is a stop, so it's Ser-Ala-Asn, then stop.

51.why: Peptide 2 is unchanged (a silent mutation). Peptide 3 hits an early stop codon (nonsense), making a short, likely useless protein.
